newsitem.title: JAPAN: Russian tanker spillage pollutes more Japan coast.
newsitem.headline: Russian tanker spillage pollutes more Japan coast.

text.p: Headaches of those battling one of Japan's worst ever oil disasters worsened on Thursday as massive new slicks whipped by heavy winds came ashore across more than 300 km (190 miles) of once-pristine coastline.
The area of coast spanning four prefectures facing the Sea of Japan around Kyoto includes some of Japan's most fertile fishing areas as well as small ports and tourist resorts.
The band of oil had reached the coastline of Hyogo Prefecture by Thursday morning, about 160 km (100 miles) away from where the bow of the ruptured tanker Nakhodka washed up on to rocks.
"It's worse than what we expected," said one fisherman cleaning up the shores at Imagoura in Hyogo Prefecture.
"We have to scoop the oil by hand because the slick is jelly-like and won't react to neutralising chemicals or absorbing mats," a Hyoyo prefectural official said.

Normally thriving fish markets along the shore of the fishing port town of Mikuni in Fukui Prefecture were either shut or had only frozen or processed seafood on sale, a rare sight in fish-loving Japan.
The cleanup operation was still mainly dependent on manual labour, with local residents continuing to scoop up oil from the shore by hand, while cranes hauled out oil-filled barrels.
The Transport Ministry has dispatched an oil salvage ship towards Wakasa Bay off Kyoto Prefecture to prevent a further spreading of the damage, maritime officials said.
The Russian government has also sent a ship to help collect the oil, Japan's chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters.

Authorities still do not know the full extent of the leakage, or the potential damage it could cause. They initially estimated that 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil leaked from the tanker but on Tuesday said this figure appeared too low.
The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was carrying a total of 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
Japan's worst oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil were spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata on the Japan Sea.

Wildlife authorities have reported several cases of seagulls and other birds coated with oil from the latest spill but there have been few reports of harm to wildlife other than fish, seaweed and shellfish.
"We have had one or two reports of dead birds at several places along the...affected areas but nothing serious so far," an official of the Maritime Safety Agency said.
But wildlife experts warned that the toll could grow as the oil became more dispersed.
Hugh Parker, London representative of the International Tanker Owners' Pollution Federation Ltd, who arrived in Japan to survey the scene, said the cleanup work was going very well.
"It is more advanced than I thought it would be," he said.
